full_judgment: 16. It is true that the right of appeal is not a mere matter of procedure but is a substantive right which vests in a litigant of a law suit or action on the date of filing of the suit. It is also true that in filing appeal, the appellant has to show that the judgment and order of the trial Court is wrong and perverse. On the other hand, the law provides that if the judgment and order/decree is passed on the consent of the parties then no appeal lies against such consented judgment and order/decree. Section 96(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides "No appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the Court with the consent of the parties". Which means the parties to an action can expressly or by implication waive or forego their right of appeal by any lawful agreement or com-promise or even by conduct. If that be so, the parties to such action are barred from challenging the judgment and order/ decree passed by the Court with the con-sent of the parties. This view finds support in the case of Parveen Banu Vs. BHBFC reported in 42 DLR(AD) 234. The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Katikara Chintamani Dora and others Vs. Guatreddi Annamanaidu and others reported in AIR 1974 SC 1069 in paragraph 56 held "Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure not only permits a partial compromise and adjustment of a suit by a lawful agreement, but further gives a mandate to the court to, record it and pass a decree in terms of such com-promise or adjustment in so far as it relates to the suit. If the compromise 4 agreement was lawful and as we shall presently discuss it was so the decree to the extent it was a consent decree, was not appealable because of the express bar in Section 96 (3) of the Code."
